main_issue: The three supplied cases consistently support unsafe Java object deserialization, but the guideline includes irrelevant resource/principal/destination-binding language and overstates signature checks as a general deserialization defense; it should focus on attacker-influenced bytes reaching general-purpose object reconstruction before an effective type or format restriction.
suggested_guideline: Trace attacker-influenced bytes into Java ObjectInputStream.readObject(), Kryo, or equivalent general-purpose deserializers that can instantiate attacker-selected classes or object graphs. Report paths that deserialize before enforcing an allowlist or ObjectInputFilter, a strict expected-type check, size and graph limits, or a data-only schema. Verify the restriction is applied before object construction and covers nested classes and callbacks. Prefer manual parsing or schema-bound data formats when untrusted input does not require arbitrary object reconstruction.
evidence_notes: CVE-2025-47771 explicitly creates ObjectInputStream from a supplied InputStream and calls readObject() without filtering or validation.
CVE-2021-32634 is labeled CWE-502 and its PayloadUtil and WorkBundle anchors are consistent with insecure object/payload deserialization.

CVE-2025-32897 has serializer/deserializer anchors across Seata Raft snapshot and sync-message paths; the supplied metadata is consistent with the family, although no trace evidence identifies the precise deserializer API or attacker-controlled ingress.
The cluster summary mentions a System.exit outlier, but no such outlier appears among the three assigned case examples; that statement should not influence this group judgment.
